prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: Customer Onboarding Field Validation Rules (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Field" · longest unbreakable unit 126px · widest one-line content 126px
  col 2: header "Pattern" · longest unbreakable unit 114px · widest one-line content 1074px
  col 3: header "Example valid" · longest unbreakable unit 167px · widest one-line content 264px
  col 4: header "Error message" · longest unbreakable unit 157px · widest one-line content 700px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 360px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). At 360px some words cannot fit unsplit. Horizontal scrolling is ALLOWED: the table may be wider than 360px (column widths summing to more than 359px) (the reader scrolls), or you may fit within 359px and accept the consequences. Fitting and scrolling layouts are judged as two separate classes; propose good layouts of BOTH kinds.
Rendering convention: a full render shows the WHOLE table; anything right of the dashed box is not clipped — it is reached by scrolling. Where a layout scrolls, an extra "viewport view" image shows only what is visible at first sight.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Provide a reference for validating customer onboarding fields, with a pattern, valid example, and user-facing error message for each field.","tasks":["Find a field and read its validation rule, example, and error message across the row.","Compare patterns and constraints across fields when implementing or checking validation.","Read error messages and examples to understand the expected input."],"relations":["Each row connects one field identifier to its regex, a valid value, and the message shown when validation fails.","The example and error message explain the same constraints expressed more compactly by the regex."],"roles":["The first column identifies rows; the remaining columns contain the pattern, example, and error message for each field.","The header labels each column; the seven body rows have equal structural importance."],"keep_whole":["Field identifiers, regex tokens and syntax, example values, numbers, and meaningful units such as YYYY-MM-DD where space permits.","The long email regex is wider than a phone viewport even before the other columns are included."],"may_wrap":["Error messages can wrap at natural word boundaries.","Patterns and long examples may need to wrap at available break points in compact layouts, with some identifiers or tokens splitting in a viewport-fitting layout."],"same_scale":["All field identifiers share one column scale; examples and error messages should each remain consistent within their own columns.","Pattern and prose columns need different widths because their content and reading tasks differ."],"h_vs_v":"Fitting all four columns on a phone makes every column narrower than its longest unbreakable content and produces extensive splitting and tall rows. Scrolling preserves identifiers and gives examples and messages usable reading widths, at the cost of moving horizontally to connect information across each row."}
